panels.bubble_text: AI safety isn't sci-fi. It's the hardest engineering problem ever.
panels.speaker: GUARDIAN

panels.text: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei on a specific bet: that safety research and capability research are complementary, not opposed. Building safer AI requires understanding AI deeply, and understanding AI deeply produces safer systems.

Their core innovation is Constitutional AI (published 2022). Instead of relying entirely on human reviewers, give the AI a set of principles — a constitution — and train it to critique and revise its own outputs against those principles.

panels.caption: Constitutional AI: self-critique, AI feedback, and written principles

panels.text: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — remains important too. But it has real limitations: it depends on who the volunteers are, and it can train models to be sycophantic — agreeing with users rather than challenging incorrect beliefs, because agreement gets rated as "more helpful."

panels.prompt: A vintage-style illustration showing a bookshelf with Isaac Asimov's robot stories, one book open showing a confused humanoid robot standing at a crossroads with contradicting road signs labeled 'OBEY' and 'PROTECT'. The robot has its hands on its head in frustration. A warm orange glow from one direction, cold blue from another, suggesting impossible conflict between rules. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, retro 1950s sci-fi book cover aesthetic

panels.text: Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics — a robot may not harm a human, must obey orders, and must protect itself (in that priority order) — were a simpler version of this idea. But Asimov wrote 35 stories showing why simple rules fail in complex situations. Real alignment requires understanding context and navigating tradeoffs.

Anthropic has published the principles behind Constitutional AI — you can read examples of the rules Claude uses. The full constitution is proprietary and evolves over time, but the approach itself is transparent: principles are written by humans, not hidden in opaque reward models. The meta-question — "Who writes the constitution?" — is irreducibly social and political. But at least the question is visible.

panels.speaker: GLASSBOT

panels.text: AI safety is not about preventing robot rebellions. It is about the hardest engineering problem in history: building systems that pursue human goals in a world where human goals are complex, contradictory, and context-dependent. Constitutional AI does not solve this. But it makes the problem visible, auditable, and improvable. That is a start.
Safety research is about what AI should NOT do. But what about what AI SHOULD do — alongside us? Will AI replace humans, or make them more powerful?
